title: Ozzy the orphaned long-nosed potoroo loves his peanuts
text:
Ozzy, the long-nosed potoroo, is living his best life in the eco-sanctuary of Tatachilla Lutheran College in the famous wine-growing region of McLaren Vale, just south of Adelaide.

In January, his life was in the balance after his mother became ill with a bacterial infection and had to be euthanised.

Still in the pouch, weighing 96 grams and having only just grown his first covering of fur, a team of staff, students and volunteers pulled together to help raise him.

Ozzy, the long-nosed potoroo, having one of his two-early feeds in the early days of his care when he weighed less than 100 grams. (Supplied: Tatachilla Lutheran College)

They included long-standing staff member Dolores Amos, who prefers to be known as Ranger Dee, who took on the two-hourly night feeds and resultant sleep deprivation needed to keep him alive.

During the day, other staff and volunteers kept up with his feeds, and students helped by crocheting pouches to keep little Ozzy feeling warm and safe.

Ozzy was orphaned after his mother developed a bacterial infection. (Supplied: Tatachilla Lutheran College)

Now Ozzy is a healthy one-kilogram juvenile.

Tom Hurley, the coordinator of the college's EcoSanctuary, said Ozzy's development was a testament to Ranger Dee's skills and knowledge.

" He's grown into a very robust young male. "

Ozzy is now one of 20 long-nosed potoroos living in the eco-sanctuary and now weighs one kilogram. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

Growing independence

Now, in what could be called his teenage phase, Ozzy has moved out of the care centre and is becoming an independent resident of the school's 4.3ha eco-sanctuary.

While he is learning "how to be a proper potoroo", he still has an appetite for a peanut treat.

Ranger Dee and the other staff have to resist the urge to give Ozzy too many peanut treats. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

He still comes when called in the early morning, but it takes him a while to rouse after spending much of the night foraging for roots, fungi, grubs, and insects.

Recently, Ozzy has started making a nest for himself under a bus, a sign that he's starting to have female potoroos on his mind.

Hopefully he will find one amongst the nine other potoroos that live with him, in addition to the brush-tailed bettongs, tammar wallabies, and birds that can flourish away from the threat of cats and foxes.

Students at the college crocheted pouches to keep Ozzy warm and secure. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

The college's eco-sanctuary is more than 20 years old and is on land that was once used to grow grapes and run sheep in the famous wine-growing region of McLaren Vale.

It's been revegetated with plants native to the local area and fenced to keep out cats, foxes and other predators, which is just as well for Ozzy and the other potoroos that call the sanctuary home, as Mr Hurley said they tended to be "incredibly naive" to these threats.

Ranger Dee, Tom Hurley and Tatachilla Lutheran College Principal Alison Thacker with Ozzy. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

The sanctuary is used as a teaching resource and as a place for students who want to learn about the environment, providing a contrast between what the area was once like and the vineyards that surround the school.

"This is as close to what it used to be like, as we can create," Mr Hurley said.

Lost to the wild in South Australia

Rob Brewster from the Invasive Species Council said he believed long-nosed potoroos were extinct in the wild in South Australia, due to land clearing and the introduction of feral predators.

Rob Brewster said long-nosed potoroos were believed to be extinct in the wild in South Australia. (ABC News: Lani Oataway)

While they were able to cope with native predators such as quolls, the potoroos had not been able to withstand cats and foxes, as well as the loss of complex vegetation.

He said that while the school's population of potoroos was only small, it meant a lot to keep the species "on the radar" and show how they could be returned to South Australia "one day".

Letting go

The time will come soon when Ranger Dee calls for Ozzy, but he'll no longer respond as he gets on with his life, safe within the sanctuary, and she's not fazed.

Ozzy has graduated from two-hourly feeds to foraging for himself. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

"That's the way it should be," she said.

Holding the pouch she had made for Ozzy when he was smaller, Year 11 student Marlee felt the same way.

"To see him now, out with the rest of the animals, is so sweet."

title: Cyclist, 19, dies during Volta a Portugal after collision with vehicle
text:
A 19-year-old British cyclist has been killed in an accident during the eighth stage of the Volta a Portugal.

Welsh rider Finlay Tarling died after "a collision between the cyclist and a light goods vehicle", Major Tiago Machado of the National Republican Guard said in a statement.

An investigation is underway, according to local authorities.

Tarling, the younger brother of Netcompany-Ineos rider Josh, had raced for Great Britain on the road and track.

He was competing for the NSN Development Team when the incident occurred on the 166.8-kilometre route from Melgaco to Fafe.

Riders are seen in Fafe, Portugal, reacting to the news that Finlay Tarling had died. (Getty Images: Miguel Lemos/NurPhoto)

In a statement, NSN said the team was heartbroken to announce Tarling's passing.

"Fin was a much-loved member of our team but most importantly, he was a son, a brother, and a friend to so many. He will be deeply missed.

"Our deepest condolences go out to Fin's parents Michael and Dawn, his brother Josh, and everyone who was lucky enough to call Fin a friend."

The intrinsic failings and risks of cycling laid bare with another premature death Cycling has lost another rider due to a downhill crash, with teenager Muriel Furrer killed on a descent at the World Championships in Zurich. So where does the responsibility lie?

In a post on X, the race organisers and the Portuguese Cycling Federation also expressed their "most heartfelt condolences to the family of Finlay Tarling, to his team-mates, to the NSN Development Team, and to all his friends and loved ones".

It added that the racing was stopped and the scheduled podium ceremony would not take place as a sign of "respect and mourning".

Portuguese president António José Seguro said that Tarling's death had "plunged the peloton, the tournament and the host nation into mourning".

British Cycling's performance director Stephen Park added: "All of us at British Cycling are heartbroken to learn of the tragic passing of Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal.

"Fin was a talented rider with a fantastic future ahead of him, a loyal teammate and an all-round brilliant young man.

"Our deepest sympathies are with his parents and brother, Josh, at this tragic time."

title: Western Sydney's new $195m 'cultural institution' gets opening date
text:
The $915 million Powerhouse Parramatta will open its doors to the public on November 7, becoming Western Sydney's first state cultural institution.

The New South Wales government in May announced that construction of the museum had been completed four years after work began.

Seven expansive zones are part of the museum, including an 18-metre-high space of more than 2,200 square metres, which will feature Task Eternal, the largest exhibition about space exploration in Australia.

Inside the new Powerhouse Parramatta. (ABC News: Digby Werthmuller)

NSW Arts Minister John Graham said the opening marked the most significant cultural infrastructure project since the Sydney Opera House.

"It's a big moment for arts and culture in the west of Sydney," he said.

"The good news is it's also free, so for people under a bit of cost-of-living pressure, they'll be able to come in and see this incredible building, this great cultural institution for free.

"There's no easy way to build new cultural institutions, just as the building of the Opera House was controversial. As it proceeded, when the doors swung open, no-one was in doubt that this was an incredible addition to our city.

"I think the reaction from the public will be the same as they see this incredible building on the banks of the river right in the heart of Parramatta."

The first five exhibitions will showcase more than 3,000 objects, with more than 1,600 from the Powerhouse's own collection, with others sourced from collections around the world.

The first exhibition, Task Eternal, will include the historic Qantas Avro 504k aircraft.

The second major exhibition, announced today, The Mall, examines the history, evolution and cultural significance of the shopping mall.

Lisa Havilah says the museum is "built for the future". (ABC News: Helena Burke)

Powerhouse CEO Lisa Havilah said she was "thrilled" to announce the opening date.

"Powerhouse Parramatta is a museum built for the future, where local knowledge meets global perspectives," she said.

"We are thrilled to be opening our doors this November with five world-class exhibitions and a program that is as bold and diverse as the communities it serves."

title: Ex-minister stands by staffer's stat dec over claims of inconsistencies
text:
Former Tasmanian minister Jane Howlett says she stands by a statutory declaration she tabled in parliament on behalf of a former staffer, despite claims over inconsistencies.

Ms Howlett appeared at a parliamentary hearing into caretaker conventions on Friday, during which she was questioned over her office's knowledge of messaging that breached election guidelines.

During last year's election campaign, government business Tasracing sent out messaging to its members speaking favourably of the Liberal party's TasInsure policy.

Emails obtained by the ABC under right to information provisions show her former chief of staff Luke Gaetani had been made aware of the message before it was sent out.

Jane Howlett says she does not recall what she told Tasracing about the Liberals' signature election policy, TasInsure. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

In response, Ms Howlett — who was racing minister — tabled a statutory declaration from Mr Gaetani in which he said he was not aware of Tasracing's intention to issue any public communications about TasInsure.

But at a hearing in June, Tasracing's communications consultant Nic Turner provided further emails that had been sent to Mr Gaetani titled "message to industry".

On Friday, Ms Howlett was questioned about the accuracy of the statutory declaration.

Dean Winter, Labor: "You also believe the stat dec is still accurate, is that correct?" Jane Howlett: "I'm not going to comment on that. It's Mr Gaetani's stat dec, he stands by that, Mr Winter." Dean Winter: "If you're not going to correct the record, I guess I have to assume you also stand by the stat dec because if you didn't, you'd have to withdraw it." Jane Howlett: "I will need to seek some advice on that, Mr Winter."

She later told the hearing that "there is no evidence that it's false".

The hearing earlier heard evidence from Tasracing chief executive officer Andrew Jenkins that he heard details of the TasInsure policy from Ms Howlett over the phone.

Ms Howlett said she did not recall the conversation.

Facebook post still up, despite assurances

At the time, Tasracing published a statement on its website speaking positively of the TasInsure policy, which Ms Howlett then shared on her Facebook page.

She earlier said she was unaware of the post until it was brought to her attention in parliament in December.

Premier Jeremy Rockliff asked the head of the state service to investigate multiple claims regarding election guideline breaches. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Ms Howlett told the hearing the post had been deleted; however it was still there on Friday.

Ms Howlett: "I removed the post and corrected the record as soon as I was able to." Mr Winter: "The post and the comment are still there today." Ms Howlett: "I thought I'd removed them … I would have to through and have a look." Mr Winter: "I just did, it's still there."

Head of Tasmania's state service, Kathrine Morgan-Wicks, found the Tasracing messaging breached election guidelines and recommended staff receive training.

Investigation into staffer campaign claims

Ms Morgan-Wicks is now investigating a second matter regarding election guidelines.

Last month, former staffer Sharee Minnikin-Smith told the hearing that she was asked to carry out election campaigning for Ms Howlett in 2024, despite being employed as a taxpayer-funded advisor for another Liberal MP.

She said her work was "100 per cent for Jane Howlett" during office hours.

Sharee Minnikin-Smith was employed as a ministerial staffer, but claims she was instead made to work on Jane Howlett's election campaign. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Staffers are not allowed to undertake party political activities as part of their jobs, according to the Integrity Commission.

Ms Howlett told the hearing that Ms Morgan-Wicks is investigating this evidence; the government has disputed Ms Minnikin-Smith's claims.

Ms Howlett was questioned about whether taxpayer resources were used to aid her 2024 campaign in Lyons, as alleged by Ms Minnikin-Smith under parliamentary privilege.

Ms Howlett said all work was voluntary, as a secretary of a Liberal Party branch.

Ms Howlett: "Ms Minnikin-Smith was a member of the party and believer of our great party, and she did volunteer work." Mr Winter: "Did she use public resources to support your campaign … to your knowledge?" Ms Howlett: "I don't know if she used public resources or not, I was out campaigning every day, seven days a week, seven nights. The campaign was managed by the party."

Ms Minnikin-Smith also claimed she was told to use her parliamentary email address to send an email to Tasman Peninsula constituents the day before the election titled "A strong plan for the Tasman region".

Ms Howlett read out a text message from Ms Minnikin-Smith from the following day which read: "I have done Tasman and it has gone from my parliament email, how do I change it?"

"That indicates she made an error, like many people do," Ms Howlett told the hearing.

title: Hopes 'mini guts' will help researchers treat inflammatory bowel disease
text:
Ronan Somers looks like any other 12-year-old boy, but he has been battling a hidden illness.

At times, his ulcerative colitis has stopped him from doing the things he loves.

"I couldn't do a lot of stuff because I felt very tired," he said.

"It just made my stomach hurt and cramp and when I tried to do exercise it would hurt, and I'd go to the toilet six times a day, and that was really hard for me."

Ulcerative colitis is one of the two major types of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), the other being Crohn's disease.

It is marked by inflammation and ulceration in the large intestine, causing at times painful and debilitating gastrointestinal symptoms.

There is no cure, but it can be managed with medication.

Ronan Somers says at times, IBD has stopped him from being able to do things a 12-year-old typically would. (ABC News: Steve Martin)

Ronan has missed one in five days at school this year due to illness and medical appointments.

The road to diagnosis and then finding the right treatment has been long and difficult.

"It was a disease we'd never heard of before, so it was a new journey to us," Ronan's mother Jasmin Alarcon said.

She said it took 904 days after diagnosis for doctors to finally pinpoint the treatment that would work for him.

"He went on a lot of medication that didn't work, so it was a bit of a of trial-and-error stage," she said.

Researchers create 'mini guts'

Ronan's long journey to remission — a state of having symptoms under control — is a common trajectory that scientists at Monash University are hoping to turn around.

For the first time, using human samples, they have developed tiny 3D models of individual paediatric IBD patients' intestinal lining, stored separately to and alongside its accompanying bacteria.

The organoids, nicknamed "mini guts", are a game-changing research tool.

"The benefit is it allows us to study the disease in living tissue in the lab so we don't have to go to the patient, but it also allows us to develop and test new therapies," lead researcher Helen Abud said.

Professor Helen Abud says the "mini guts" are a game-changer for researchers. (ABC News: Nathan O'Brien)

Researchers have also been able to create technology to inject that same gut bacteria back into the patients' organoid models, something that gives paediatric gastroenterologist Associate Professor Edward Giles optimism.

"[We can] really try to understand in a very detailed way the interaction between the bacteria and the lining of the bowel to see if we can understand what's driving inflammation and also understand potential new targets for treatment," Dr Giles said.

3D models help researchers study the disease in living tissue in the lab, allowing them to develop and test new therapies. (Supplied: Monash University)

The hope is that the advancement will enable research that leads to more precise and tailored treatments for patients.

"We're starting to have great ability to understand some of the complexity in this disease because, unfortunately, it is complex and very individual," Dr Giles, who co-authored the research paper, said.

"We do have good treatments, but there is a huge onus on patients to go through this process, and we aren't very good at targeting the right treatment to the right patient at the beginning of their journey."

Edward Giles co-authored the research paper. (ABC News: Nathan O'Brien)

The team has created a "living bio bank" of several different organoids, based on several different patients.

"The overall goal is to find the best treatment for each individual patient so we need to have a replica of a whole diversity of individual patients," Professor Abud said.

"And this patient population is from our local paediatric Australian patients, so it's going to be relevant to patients that are being treated here."

IBD prevalence growing

Australian National University School of Medicine and Psychology Emeritus Professor Paul Pavli described the research as "exciting".

"It is a very important study. It's meticulous work, it's painstaking and it's going to provide very valuable insight into the cause of some of these diseases," he said.

"This is early days yet, but the point is they're beginning to tease out how normal bacteria and how the bacteria that are obtained from Crohn's and colitis patients cause abnormalities in both normal mini guts and mini guts derived from Crohn's and colitis patients."

Dr Pavli, who also works as a consultant in gastroenterology at Canberra Hospital, said it would enable medical professionals and researchers to understand the basic mechanisms of how the bacteria and the lining of the gut cause inflammation, and could lead to personalised medical care.

"This is leading towards personalised medicine where you can actually identify the things that go wrong that cause inflammatory bowel diseases in such patients," Dr Pavli said.

"It's not something that's going to develop in the next two or three years or even five years. It's going to take some time to develop the techniques to be able to provide any sort of personalised medicine."

IBD is estimated to affect about 180,000 Australians, and for reasons experts are not yet able to explain, that number is on the rise.

By about 2030, the number of sufferers will amount to 1 per cent of the population.

The statistics are alarming for advocates such as Leanne Raven, the chief executive at Crohn's and Colitis Australia.

Leanne Raven says IBD has the least investment in research of all chronic conditions. (ABC News: Steve Martin)

"In Australia, the prevalence and the incidence is just compounding," Ms Raven said.

"We are worried because there are so many barriers to people getting diagnosed and then getting into remission.

" For about half of the people who are diagnosed, it can take five years to get them into remission after diagnosis. "

She said a recent study by her organisation found of all chronic conditions, IBD had the lowest investment in research.

"Being able to use technology to play around and test different things and see what response you get is fantastic, really innovative work," she said.

"Research is our hope for the future."

It is something Dr Pavli agreed with, but he said the field did not receive much funding.

"Crohn's and colitis are not sexy diseases," he said.

"They're not the sorts of conditions people have heard about because … it's not dinner party conversation, so from that point of view there's not a great deal of public awareness about them.

"These conditions are quite serious conditions affecting young people significantly and anything that provides some insight into what goes wrong is going to lead to better treatments."

title: ACT's neurodiverse community 'cautiously welcomes' autism minister
text:
Neurodivergent support organisations have welcomed the creation of a dedicated autism and neurodiversity portfolio in the ACT government.

After a cabinet reshuffle following the resignation of Yvette Berry, Suzanne Orr became the Minister for Disability, Autism and Neurodiversity.

The ACT is now the first jurisdiction to include neurodiversity in a ministerial portfolio, and the second to include autism, after South Australia introduced an assistant minister for autism in 2022.

Autism Spectrum Australia (ASPECT) chief executive Jacqui Borland said the position would increase the visibility of autism across the ACT government and the community.

Jacqui Borland says she would like to see the position used to improve autistic people's outcomes across education, healthcare, employment and inclusion. (Supplied: ASPECT)

"That's important because the understanding that will grow will be of the diversity of autistic experience and the barriers that people can face in everyday life," she said.

"Of course, the understanding is one thing, but then what we hope we would see would be a translation then into practical improvements that help to make life more accessible and inclusive for autistic and neurodivergent people and their families."

Ms Borland said she would like to see the position used to improve autistic people's outcomes across education, healthcare, employment and inclusion.

"We know that there are many autistic neurodivergent people working in the government in Canberra," she said.

"So support to help those across all of those departments to be more inclusive would help those autistic neurodiverse people to be successful in their jobs, and then therefore be more successful in their everyday lives."

Calls for partnership with autistic community, specialists

Neurodivergent therapist Jacqueline Gibb said she welcomed the new position but was cautious, noting she was unsure why autism and neurodiversity were separated.

"But if it leads to real-world changes for autistic people and other people with different neurodivergences, then I'm all for it," she said.

Jacqueline Gibb created Actually Autistic Canberra, a support group for autistic adults, after noticing a lack of safe spaces. (Supplied: Jacqueline Gibb)

Ms Gibb, who is autistic herself, said she would like to see the ACT government work with the community to create autistic-led spaces.

She created Actually Autistic Canberra, a support group for autistic adults, because she noticed a lack of safe spaces.

"I would love for them to have actual partnerships with autistic people, with the autistic community," Ms Gibb said.

"Also with autistic professionals like myself who work in this space, who often do very well in delivering to autistic kids and autistic adults."

She said many in Canberra's neurodivergent community felt burnt out from advocating.

"Our community is really exhausted from all this constant having to advocate for ourselves and not being listened to," she said.

"I think we've all said it all, but we're just not being listened to."

Neurodiversity strategy a top priority

Suzanne Orr says she will prioritise developing a dedicated neurodiversity strategy and implementing the Thriving Kids model. (ABC News: Adam Shirley)

Ms Orr said the new portfolio aligned with the ACT government's work to progress greater disability inclusion.

"It's fair to say there is a growing focus on autism and looking at how we can better respond to autism and make an inclusive world for everybody with autism," she told 666 ABC Canberra last month.

" But autism is not the only form of neurodivergence. There's quite a bit there. "

Model released for NDIS alternative for some autistic children The federal government reveals how its NDIS alternative for some children under nine will work.

Ms Orr said one of her priorities would be developing a dedicated neurodiversity strategy, one of the government's election promises.

She said she would also be working to implement the federal government's Thriving Kids model, aiming to divert children under nine with "mild to moderate" developmental delays and autism from the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS).

"Another key priority will be working with the community and across government on the roll out of Thriving Kids services and supports to ensure children aged up to eight with autism and their parents, carers and kin with low or moderate support needs have services specific to their needs," Ms Orr said in a statement.

'Underlying uncertainty' about Thriving Kids

Jacqueline Gibb says the neurodivergent community has been critical of the Thriving Kids program.

The ACT government committed to rolling out Thriving Kids from October, over the next 18 months.

Ms Gibb said the neurodivergent community had been critical of Thriving Kids, describing it as "tokenistic".

"It feels very much like control is being taken away from the community in terms of what we can do, who we can choose, who do we work with," she said.

"It just feels very poorly thought out, and it's constantly being presented as: 'This is such a great thing for you. We're doing this as a favour to autistic people. This will be better for them.'

"I don't even know how you can really engage with an argument like that, honestly, when it's just not true."

Federal Disability and NDIS Minister Mark Butler announced the Thriving Kids program in a National Press Club address in August last year. (ABC News: Tobias Hunt)

Ms Borland said there was an "underlying uncertainty" from parents about what Thriving Kids would mean for them.

"When families don't have information, then they imagine the worst," she said.

"In terms of [Thriving Kids'] design … it's about really making sure that families who have children with developmental delays or developmental concerns through this period of transition to Thriving Kids don't fall through the gaps, that they do receive the services.

" If they will no longer be eligible for NDIS, then we need to make sure that they are supported and that there isn't a group of families through this transition who miss out. "

Ms Orr convened two roundtables with service providers, advocates, parents and carers earlier in the year to identify gaps in the ACT's support system.

"The ACT government will continue consultation and community engagement activities as planning for and implementation of Thriving Kids progresses," she said.

Suzanne Orr says the ACT government will continue consultation and community engagement about the planning and implementation of Thriving Kids. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

Ms Borland said ASPECT had been involved in the consultation process.

She said it was important Thriving Kids was designed in partnership with neurodivergent people, and support services that worked with them.

"We have talked to them about the services that we know work in terms of supporting families, in terms of supporting young children that Thriving Kids covers, in terms of supporting and providing support for the mainstream community places where those children live, work and play," Ms Borland said.

Ms Orr said the discussion around Thriving Kids had brought autism into the government's broader consciousness.

"In doing this, what we really want to do is send that signal to people that the government is focused on this area and we are committed to doing what we can to make sure that we're including people with autism neurodivergence within our community," she said.

title: Bezos consortium enters 'definitive agreement' to buy Liverpool stake
text:
A consortium containing Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin is buying a minority stake in Premier League club Liverpool, the English soccer giant says.

Club owner Fenway Sports Group (FSG) said in a statement it entered into a "definitive agreement" for the sale to 1892 Holdings.

The investor group is led by Amit Bhatia, who is married to a daughter of Indian steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal, and has taken a stake of more than 30 per cent in the 20-time English champion. The deal reportedly values Liverpool at around $US6 billion ($8.4 billion).

Boston-based FSG paid $US400 million to take over Liverpool in 2010 and also owns the Boston Red Sox. FSG said in July that it had been approached by the Bhatia-led consortium regarding a "strategic minority investment" in the club.

Eduardo Saverin is part of the investment group with Jeff Bezos. (Getty Images: Sam Barnes/Sportsfile)

"As we considered this opportunity, it became clear that Amit and the consortium shared our long-term philosophy and appreciation for what makes Liverpool special," FSG president Mike Gordon said in the statement.

It marks the first foray into soccer by Bezos, who, according to Forbes, is the fourth-richest person in the world with a net worth of about $US280 billion. He founded Amazon in 1994 and has been executive chairman since 2021.

Saverin is a Brazilian businessman worth about $US36 billion, according to Forbes.

Bhatia, a British-Indian entrepreneur, was the co-owner of second-tier English team Queens Park Rangers for 18 years before stepping down recently.

Amit Bhatia during his time as the chairman of Queens Park Rangers. (Getty Images: Steven Paston/PA Images)

"We are making this investment because we believe deeply in Liverpool and its leadership, and we look forward to supporting the club's continued success for years to come," Bhatia said in the statement.

Under the leadership of FSG and its principal owner John Henry, Liverpool ended a 30-year wait to be English champion in 2020 and added another Premier League title last year. That tied Manchester United on 20 English top-flight league championships.

The club was European champion for a sixth time — a record for an English team — in 2019.

The Premier League is one of the biggest competitions in sports, with its teams now largely owned by oil-rich Gulf states or private equity.

Liverpool sack manager Arne Slot after underwhelming season The Dutchman won the Premier League title in his first season, but failed to live up to expectations the following year as Liverpool finished fifth.

Liverpool now has three of the richest people in the world as minority owners.

That does not mean, however, that the club can simply start spending recklessly in the transfer market on new players.

That is because the Premier League has financial rules in place to protect the competitive balance of the competition and ensure the financial sustainability of clubs.

In broad terms, a club's on-pitch spending is related to 85 per cent of its "football-related revenue and net profit/loss from player sales," the Premier League says.

Instead, the difference will come in how Liverpool — already one of the top teams in world soccer — is marketed more around the world under Bezos and Saverin, especially.

The deal is likely to bring more commercial revenue into the club, thereby improving its profits.

title: Community remembers those lost in one of Australia's worst mining disasters
text:
By a quiet road, near an abandoned mine in Victoria's central highlands is a new sign detailing one of Australia's worst mining disasters.

It tells the tale of 22 men who lost their lives in the pursuit of gold 140 years ago while working at The New Australasian No.2 Mine near Creswick.

The sign, installed by the Creswick Connect community group, will ensure these 22 souls will never be forgotten and serve as a reminder of the human cost behind Victoria's gold rush.

New interpretive signage aims to preserve the stories of the disaster for future generations. (ABC News: Ava Ross)

Deep personal connection

Mining historian and guide Darren Bellingham has a deep personal connection to the No.2 Mine.

On the evening of December 11, 1882, Darren's great-great-grandfather Jabez Bellingham and great-great-uncle Benjamin Bellingham began their usual night shift working in the mine.

Darren Bellingham's great-great-grandfather Jabez Bellingham. (Supplied: Darren Bellingham)

Around 5.30am the following day, they were about to knock-off when disaster struck.

Miners were digging near an abandoned shaft that had previously flooded after it was thought all the gold had been exhausted.

While they were working, a geological disturbance caused water to surge into the mine, blocking the way out and trapping 29 men almost a kilometre from the entrance.

With the clock ticking and the water rising, the group decided the men with more children were allowed to go up ladders so they could keep out of the water for longer.

The New Australasian No.2 Mine near Creswick. (Supplied: Mitchell Library)

A small number of miners managed to escape, particularly the fitter men and the stronger swimmers.

Jabez was among them, but he turned back to try and save his brother Benjamin.

The miners had found a small pocket of air, huddling together in complete darkness, about 90 metres below the surface, with only their heads above the rising water.

To keep hope alive, Jabez used his skills as the church organist and choir master to lead the men in singing, and the men prayed and sang hymns as the water rose.

Knowing rescue might never come, some scratched their final messages onto metal buckets, hoping their words would survive even if they did not.

Twenty-seven miners remained trapped underground for three days, some in the water, while huddled on timber and ladders, in a chamber roughly the size of a shipping container.

As time passed, many succumbed to exhaustion, dehydration and lack of oxygen, leaving just five survivors when rescuers finally reached them after much of the water had been pumped out.

The story of the 27 trapped miners has been preserved on signage constructed by Creswick Connect. (Supplied: James Freemantle, Creswick Connect)

The Bellingham brothers tied themselves together, fearing they might be separated if the water claimed them.

Neither man survived.

Four thousand people marched in a funeral procession for the dead miners, with 15,000 mourners watching on.

Jabez's choir sang over his grave, while Benjamin, a member of the local military corps, was honoured with a gun salute at his funeral.

An underground mine tour at Sovereign Hill offers visitors an insight into the dangerous working conditions miners had to face. (ABC News: Ava Ross)

Path to compensation

Darren Bellingham said the effects of the disaster were felt deeply across the community.

"It had a really big impact — every mine for 100 kilometres around Creswick was closed that day," Darren said.

Darren Bellingham has a deep family connection to the New Australasian No.2 Mine disaster. (ABC News: Ava Ross)

The gravity of the disaster started to make people think about compensation issues, and lack of protection for miners' families, ultimately leading to the creation of the Mining Accident Relief Fund Act two years later, which established formal compensation for victims of mining accidents.

For Darren, one detail has always stayed with his family.

"Benjamin wasn't supposed to work that day," he said.

"He took someone else's shift because he was looking for extra work, and so, he was killed and he shouldn't have been."

The memorial remembers the miners who died. (Supplied: James Freemantle, Creswick Connect)

A legacy of sacrifice

More than 140 years after one of Victoria's worst mining disasters, new interpretive signage at the site of the New Australasian No.2 Mine in Creswick aims to ensure the lives of the 22 men who died are never forgotten.

The project has been years in the making and will be officially unveiled by Creswick Connect on August 30.

Project manager James Freemantle said he hoped visitors leave with a greater appreciation and respect for the miners that helped shape what Victoria is today.

"It's so important not to forget that so many people were sacrificed," Mr Freemantle said.

"We want people to be touched by the story and to respect the lives that were lost but also think about what we ask people to do in the name of progress.

"What sacrifices do we ask people to make when you know we're trying to find profits?"

title: Luxury tower 'affordability' claim rejected in landmark court ruling
text:
A legal cloud is hanging over high-rises on the Gold Coast after a court ruled luxury apartments do not improve housing affordability simply because they increase housing supply.

The Queensland Court of Appeal ruled in July that the council's claim that a luxury high-rise would improve "housing choice and affordability" was not enough to justify exceeding the regulated height limit.

In a judgment summary, Justice Shane Doyle stated that apartments targeting the luxury market could not reasonably be considered as improvements to housing affordability.

"To add to the supply of apartments designed to cater to the luxury and more affluent market cannot, in my view, be reconciled with the ordinary meaning of the word 'affordability'," he wrote.

" To do so would be a distortion of the ordinary meaning of affordability. "

The court ruling has thrown the council's high-rise approvals into uncertainty, with councillors set to be briefed on its implications later this month.

Construction of new apartment buildings along Bilinga in January 2025. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

Luxury gets 'affordability' exemption

Under the council's planning rules, developers can build up to 50 per cent above an area's height limit if they meet a list of criteria.

Those criteria cover issues from neighbourhood amenity and design to whether a project benefits "housing choice and affordability".

In 2023, developer Cielo Property Group applied to build an almost 34-metre-high tower at Pacific Parade in Bilinga, 10 metres above the suburb's height limit.

The development was also more than double the permitted density, with one bedroom per 14.9 square metres compared with the limit of one per 33 square metres.

The site of a proposed luxury high-rise at 90–92 Pacific Parade, Bilinga. (ABC Gold COast: Dominic Cansdale)

But the City of Gold Coast approved the luxury project, finding it satisfied the exemption criteria, including by benefiting "housing choice and affordability".

Nearby residents challenged that approval in the Planning and Environment Court but lost.

Court documents state the "very expensive apartments" would not provide affordable housing for low- to moderate-income earners, but could provide a "net community benefit to a more affluent segment of the market to meet their housing needs and choices".

But the Court of Appeal found that to be "an error in law", with its ruling "expected to have significance for other development applications".

Limited definition for affordability

The Court of Appeal noted that the council's planning scheme did not directly define "housing choice and affordability".

But it did define "affordable housing" as "appropriate to the needs of households with low to moderate incomes, if the members of the households will spend no more than 30 per cent of gross income on housing costs".

The council argued that "increased density is one way to increase affordability".

Higher-density towers are set to spread further across the Gold Coast. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

But the Court of Appeal disagreed, finding that simply increasing the number of homes in a luxury development was not enough to satisfy the requirement for "housing choice and affordability".

The Bilinga project has been sent back to the Planning and Environment Court for reconsideration.

Councillors will be briefed on the implications of the Court of Appeal’s decision on August 25.

The ABC understands a High Court appeal remains open to council.

'Much wider implications'

Retired lawyer Michael Sparksman challenged another Bilinga development in the Planning and Environment Court last year, on the basis it harmed the area's character and visual amenity.

He said the court had been "waving through any luxury development" on an incorrect understanding of "housing choice and affordability".

"You can't simply say that luxury apartments are affordable — luxury apartments are in the multi-million-dollar range," Mr Sparksman said.

He said the Court of Appeal decision would have "much wider implications", especially in the southern suburbs, where height limits had become a major community concern.

High-rise developments have been met with some resistance on the southern Gold Coast. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

"It sets the tone for this interpretation to run across all councils, certainly in Queensland but especially the Gold Coast where developers and council have run roughshod," he said.

"Some existing approvals will probably be challenged."

On Tuesday, the council's Planning and Regulation Committee delayed a 40-unit luxury high-rise in Palm Beach, pending legal advice on how the Court of Appeal's ruling could affect its approval.

Deputy Mayor and committee chair Mark Hammel said council was legally obliged to continue assessing development applications under the current planning scheme, but work was underway on a new scheme.

"This reinforces for me the importance of the work we are currently doing on the new planning scheme to deliver more certainty for the community and the most efficient and effective development outcomes for residents, the development industry and the courts," he said.

Cielo Property Group has been contacted for comment.

title: Sydney Trains boss apologises after fallen wires cause network chaos
text:
Trains will operate on schedule this morning after overhead wiring issues caused widespread delays across Sydney's network last night.

Hundreds of people were assisted off trains after overhead wires came down onto one of them yesterday evening.

Significant delays across Sydney's rail network continued into the night.

Commuters had to be assisted off the South Coast service between Redfern and Erskineville after overhead wire come down on the train. (Supplied: Sean Murphy)

Sydney Trains chief executive Matt Longland said all six lines were now open.

"I want to apologise to passengers who were impacted by delays on the rail network in Sydney on Friday night," he said.

"Teams have worked right through the night last night and all six lines through the area are now fully reopened with normal weekend services operating, but a reminder that track work is in place in Western Sydney today.

"We'll be investigating the root cause of the incident throughout the weekend."

Passengers using trains this weekend are being advised that planned track work is continuing today, with changes to parts of the T2, T4, T5, Blue Mountains and South Coast lines.

About 4:30pm yesterday, the South Coast Line service was travelling between Redfern and Erskineville, in Sydney's inner west, when the wires came down.

Sydney Trains says trains will run to normal service today. (Supplied: Sean Murphy)

Two other nearby trains came to a grinding halt.

Transport authorities isolated power to safely remove passengers.

Just before 7pm last night, some commuters were still being assisted off, but everyone had been cleared by 8pm.

Sydney major train delays Hundreds of people have been assisted off trains after overhead wires came down onto one of them on Friday evening.

Earlier, Sydney Trains' head of rail operations, Jas Tumber, said the cause of the wiring issue was unknown.

"This is a really significant disruption that's causing really wide ripple effects," he said.

Train passenger Sean Murphy said he left Redfern for Sutherland on the Kiama train about 4:30pm and that "the engine just stopped" five minutes later.

"The train just went basically dead," he said.

Mr Murphy said staff announced that a train ahead of them "had brought down powerlines" and to await further instructions.

title: If WA doesn't like its GST deal, it always has the nuclear option
text:
Alarm bells were literally ringing in Western Australian government offices after the "east coast clowns" launched their attack on the state's precious GST dollars.

"While we're gone, they're going to take our GST," Treasurer Rita Saffioti joked before evacuating from a fiery press conference.

It was only partly a joke.

Journalists, politicians and staffers were forced to evacuate during the media conference. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Western Australia has relied heavily on a sweetheart deal, which replaced the formula all other states rely on, to fund its economy in recent years with an extra $22 billion from the Commonwealth up to mid-2025.

That extra money has meant WA benefited and posted record surpluses, while the rest of the nation remained no worse off.

A new interim report by the Productivity Commission said that while WA received enough GST revenue to meet 113 per cent of its assessed fiscal needs in 2024-25, compared with 98 per cent for other states, the federal government topped up the remaining 2 per cent.

WA's leaders insist that money has been more than paid back to the nation in company tax payments and the like, and that it deserves the extra billions to enable the country's prosperity.

The Productivity Commission yesterday revealed it agreed with every other state and territory, saying the deal had produced "perverse outcomes" and created a two-tier system.

WA Premier Roger Cook came out swinging, dubbing those conclusions and the proposed fixes "dodgy, deceitful and quite frankly dumb".

That the normally mild-mannered premier was so fired up can be explained by the $6 billion hit the mining state could be up for if the deal was done away with entirely. Not that that is being suggested.

Roger Cook says WA plays a vital role in the country's economy because of its unmatched resources sector. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

How much, if any, is lost depends on the commission's final recommendations later this year and whether the federal government adopts them.

It's why WA has given up trying to convince the other states of the deal's merits, whose premiers Cook today branded as "whingers", to focus on the only two people who matter: the prime minister and his treasurer.

Loading...

Next steps a matter of politics

It was politics which got the federation into this mess, and it will almost certainly be politics which decides what happens next.

The 2018 deal was struck between then-WA premier Mark McGowan and then-prime minister Scott Morrison to resolve a political headache for the new West Australian government.

The deal was struck in 2018 between Mark McGowan (left) and Scott Morrison. (ABC News: James Carmody)

A falling iron ore price, and therefore reduced royalties flowing into the state's coffers, coincided with its GST payments falling.

WA premier lashes 'east-coast clowns' An angry Roger Cook has lashed who he calls 'east-coast clowns' over an explosive proposed shake-up of the GST carve-up.

That's because the way the GST had been carved up was about putting all states on an equal footing by offering more money to those which earned less themselves, or had higher expenses, averaged out over three years to smooth things out.

That averaging meant WA's share was falling, from the previously strong years, just as its royalties dried up.

This chart shows what happened in the years since. Not only have royalties been up because of high iron ore prices, but so too have GST payments, thanks to the deal.

The current fight is really two separate debates: should WA get extra money from the Commonwealth to help fund its mining industry, and if so, how should it get it?

For the deal's chief critic, independent economist Saul Eslake, the first answer is no.

In his view, WA isn't holding up the national economy.

"Yes, Western Australia generates a lot of exports from minerals, largely thanks to China's thirst for them and its willingness to pay hitherto unimaginable prices for them," he said.

" That's not the result of any far-sighted policies by the current or previous Western Australian governments. It's good fortune. "

Aaron Morey says running WA's economy takes an incredible amount of resources from government. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

It's an idea angrily rejected by the state, which argues the only reason WA benefits from China's hunger for iron ore is because of support offered by successive governments.

"The Productivity Commission thinks that running a world-class mining sector is as easy as ordering a cafe latte on Collins Street," Chamber of Minerals and Energy boss Aaron Morey said.

"Well, I've got news for them. It ain't."

How could this be resolved?

Despite WA's complaints, the Productivity Commission isn't necessarily arguing the state shouldn't receive extra money.

Its concern is that the GST was not designed fund particular projects or government priorities, but to even out states' fiscal capacities.

Iron ore royalties and WA's GST payments are on the up. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

That's not what is happening now.

Under the current system, WA is funded to 113 per cent of its needs, according to the commission.

The commission said any move away from fully equalising states' finances could be "proposed and defended" but needed to be clearly justified and deliver benefits.

Eslake, and others, don't believe that case has been made.

The commission would rather the GST formula is adjusted, or funding is provided another way.

The latter leaves those funds open to change at the whim of the federal government.

The former is too complex, according to the WA treasurer.

"Trying to unpick this deal will disadvantage WA," Rita Saffioti told the ABC.

The fiery press conference continued outdoors. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

She also pointed out the 2018 deal is enshrined in legislation, meaning even if Labor wanted to change it the Greens or Liberals would need to agree.

Two of WA's top federal Liberals, Michaelia Cash and Andrew Hastie, said that wouldn't happen.

"Over our dead bodies will they take a cent from Western Australia," Senator Cash said.

Mr Cook said he's spoken to the PM who told him "arrangements in place for Western Australia will remain".

Basil Zempilas isn't counting on the prime minister to save the day in WA. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"Anthony Albanese, who backtracked on negative gearing, who backtracked on capital gains tax," state opposition leader Basil Zempilas said.

"How can any West Australian trust that he is not going to backtrack on what is right for West Australians when it comes to our share of the GST?"

Over to Albanese

That's one way of seeing those broken promises.

The other is that Labor might think twice about opening up another fight.

Especially when that fight would risk the WA seats which put it into power in 2022 and kept it there in 2025, at the same time as One Nation threatens to up-end the political landscape.

It's also possible the Commonwealth could try to find a way of undoing the current deal without WA losing out, at least too much.

If it all goes pear shaped though, Western Australia always has the nuclear option up its sleeve.

Anthony Albanese famously writes and signs 'No Change To WA GST' on the forearm of a journalist in 2019. (AAP: Richard Wainwright)

"Is secession tempting?" a journalist asked yesterday.

"Every Western Australian premier has that thought from time to time," Cook said.

"But it's not an option. We don't want to be separate from the rest of Australia.

"We just sincerely believe that we should not be penalised for doing the heavy lifting on economic activity."

title: Should Australia copy New Zealand's 83-page building code?
text:
Cross-party support for prefabricated and modular homes is building in Canberra as an answer to Australia's housing crisis.

The Albanese government is pouring millions of dollars into the idea. Building industry groups, think tanks, and major banks support it. And Liberal senator Andrew Bragg, the shadow minister for housing, loudly supports the idea.

With such momentum building for the policy, what does it mean for the future of Australian housing?

Liberal vows to demolish building code Opposition housing spokesperson Andrew Bragg has promised to slash the National Construction Code from over 2,000 pages to 80 if elected.

At Friday's meeting of federal, state and territory treasurers, participants were briefed on the Albanese government's plans to promote Modern Methods of Construction (MCC) to lift productivity in the construction and housing industries.

They were also given an update on the government's efforts to modernise the National Construction Code which has been long in the making.

At the end of the meeting they agreed to review the barriers to wider adoption of MMC in Australia to support manufacturing.

But earlier in the week a Senate committee also released its interim report on Australia's housing industry. The committee, chaired by Senator Bragg, is comprised of Liberal, Nationals and Labor members.

Modular homes help housing crisis The modular home model would involve sections of rooms being constructed off-site in a dedicated facility before being transported to new developments across NSW.

In a speech to the National Press Club on Wednesday, Senator Bragg talked about the recommendations in that interim report.

He used the report as a springboard to promote his own plan to slash the number of pages in the National Construction Code (NCC) and adopt "an 80-page Basic Australian Standard".

But what would Bragg's plan actually look like? Would it help or hinder reforms that are already underway?

And what does it have to do with Modern Methods of Construction and prefab housing?

What does Senator Bragg's plan look like?

The original Building Code of Australia, from 1988, was 209 pages, including a title page.

At the Press Club, Senator Bragg said the Coalition had committed to reducing the size of the modern NCC, which has grown to more than 2,200 pages, back to the size of the original BCA.

The Housing Industry Association (HIA) has been calling for such a policy.

In the HIA's submission to the Senate inquiry on housing it said Australia's government should:

"Undertake a code overhaul and regulatory reform and simplification program, setting a goal to return the code to the 208 pages that reflected the first edition of the BCA (NCC) in 1988."

And in his speech to the Press Club on Wednesday, Senator Bragg made this announcement about his committee's interim report:

"We have met the ambition of industry to get back to an NCC closer to the original 200 pages, when first created in 1988. Our new framework for an 80-page Basic Australian Standard is some 2,000 pages shorter than Labor's NCC."

That second sentence from Senator Bragg about an 80-page Basic Australian Standard led to some confusion.

In response to questions from the ABC later in the week, Senator Bragg's office clarified what his plan was.

Andrew Bragg has called for a radical overhaul of the National Construction Code. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

It said Senator Bragg wanted to introduce a new framework that would have an "80 to 90-page Basic Australian Standard" sitting within a slimmed down and simplified construction code.

So, his Basic Australian Standard would be the mandatory core requirements for building.

In the current NCC the only mandatory requirements in the code are performance requirements, and they total 200 pages, according to testimony from Simon Croft, chief executive of industry and policy at the HIA.

Is factory made a solution to housing? Prefab, modular housing has been touted as the answer to Australia's housing supply for years, but it's an industry plagued with high costs, low scale and a desperate need for investment if it's ever going to be a solution.

For Senator Bragg's plan, broader elements for building "optional extras" on a basic house would then come on top of his 80 to 90-page Basic Australian Standard.

It means you would have to familiarise yourself with 80 to 90 pages of his proposed new building code at a minimum because they would cover the essential structural, fire safety, health and basic amenity requirements, including basic energy efficiency.

If you wanted to build something more sophisticated than a basic structure you would have to read additional material to ensure that you were building everything to code.

Those "optional extras" would include things like Graduated Liveable Housing Standards, and Extended Energy Efficiency options.

The interim report from the Senate committee, which Senator Bragg chairs, has suggested that the new framework could look like this:

(Source: Senate Select Committee on Productivity in Australia, interim report: housing, August 2026, page 48.)

The interim report also says the Basic Australian Standard would be supported by a federal "pattern book" to fast-track approvals and enable innovation, including for prefabricated housing and Modern Methods of Construction (MMC).

The federal pattern book would contain pre-approved standard housing designs and allow for MMC.

The New Zealand model

After his speech to the Press Club on Wednesday, Senator Bragg was criticised by some groups for suggesting that low-income earners should accept substandard housing built to the most basic code.

On the ABC's Radio National he was asked: "Are you suggesting that to afford housing, some low-income Australians will have to accept housing that is substandard?"

Senator Bragg replied: "Yes, definitely. And I think we've got to be clear there are trade-offs here … if it's more important to have a house than to not have a house.

"So given the affordability crisis we have in the housing system we need to just build more houses," he said.

Loading...

But on Friday afternoon, Senator Bragg said he had misheard the question about housing standards and he did not mean to suggest that houses built to his Basic Australian Standard would be "substandard".

"Houses built to this standard would be strong, safe and sound homes with all the basic amenity, such as insulation, plumbing, sewerage etc. This position has been strongly backed by the industry," he posted on X (formerly Twitter).

His ideas were inspired by the HIA, which has been arguing that Australia should adopt New Zealand's slimmed-down building code model, and the HIA has not said that low-income earners should accept substandard housing.

Factory-built homes could help Australia reindustrialise, report says Factory-built homes could solve Australia's housing crisis and drive reindustrialisation, report says.

The HIA says New Zealand's Building Code is 83 pages long but it is underpinned by a broad range of compliance solutions that are attached to the mandatory code.

The HIA imagines that a new NCC compliance structure for Australia could look like the graphic below.

Its proposed model begins at the top of the graphic with an 83-page mandatory building code, and then you read your way through various "pathways" to suit the type of structure you want to build:

(Source: Housing Industry Association, answer to written question on notice, 4 May 2026, received 19 May 2026, to Select Committee on Productivity in Australia.)

The HIA's graphic looks very similar to the dashboard for New Zealand's building code.

How to use Modern Methods of Construction

On the specific topic of Modern Methods of Construction (MMC), the Senate committee's interim report said the federal government should embrace MMC, prefabricated housing and modular homes to build houses more cheaply and quickly.

It puts Senator Bragg and his Coalition colleagues on the same page as the Albanese government and building industry groups which are already investigating MMC as a potential way to boost productivity in the building industry.

This is how the Australian Building Codes Board explains what MMC is:

Modern methods of construction (MMC) refers to a range of construction methods that are different to traditional onsite construction. This includes prefabrication, off-site manufacturing, and modular or volumetric dwellings, as well as new technologies such as 3D printing, robotics, and artificial intelligence. MMC have the potential to support the delivery of higher quality buildings and increase productivity in the construction sector. The Productivity Commission reported that prefabricated and modular construction can reduce the cost of homes by up to 20 per cent. Prefabricated and modular homes can be up to 50 per cent faster to construct than homes built using traditional methods of construction. MMC technologies encourage increased productivity and efficient building processes, resulting from greater speed and accuracy. Prefabricated and modular construction can also offer improved certainty, safety, quality and environmental sustainability benefits.

But the Coalition and Labor may have different visions for what MMC could be used for.

The John Curtin Research Centre, a Labor-aligned think tank, says the federal government could use MMC and prefab homes to rebuild and revitalise Australia's broader manufacturing sector.

For just $1 a design, expect to see these homes pop up across Sydney These housing designs are focused on densifying the suburbs and fast-tracking low-rise housing throughout Sydney and beyond.

It says MMC could be part of an ambitious national strategy that would help Australia to rebuild its industrial base in a once-in-a-generation opportunity to reverse decades of deindustrialisation and underwrite a housing construction boom.

It released a report on the topic recently that explained how that ambition could be realised.

Federal Housing Minister Clare O'Neil launched that report at Labor's National Conference last month.

Growing support for MMC

There is also growing support from industry and building groups for wider adoption of MMC and prefab housing, which suggests that the future of housing in Australia may look quite different from today.

Urban Taskforce Australia wants the government to support the adoption of modular and prefabricated housing, and to remove regulatory barriers to help the building industry make the transition.

Are 'flatpack' homes Australia's future? From early colonial settlers to the post-war construction boom, prefabricated and modular housing has a long history in Australia. Can factory-built homes fix our housing woes and help the climate?

Engineers Australia says the government should promote MMC to support off-site manufacturing for faster, cleaner, and more resilient construction, with clear guidance and approval processes.

Treasury says the Albanese government's National Competition Policy agenda is focused on "streamlining and aligning regulation, in areas including Modern Methods of Construction".

The Australian Building Codes Board (ABCB) has been asked by the federal government to develop a national voluntary certification scheme for manufacturers of prefabricated construction.

title: Elie’s family business was on death row. He turned it into a global juggernaut
text:
Advertisement

NationalNSWImmigration Elie’s family business was on death row. He turned it into a global juggernaut Mostafa Rachwani August 15, 2026 — 10:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There were many moments in his life where Dr Aniss Chami believed his father had lost his mind. But the most jaw-dropping moment was when the elder Chami revealed to his family that he had decided to convert his small packing facility in Prestons in Sydney’s south-west into a pharmaceutical manufacturer. From top: Lucie, Latify, Anthony, Aniss, Robine and Elie Chami turned around their company’s fortunes. Sitthixay Ditthavong The Lebanese-Australian family were on the verge of ruin after the collapse of a key supplier put their fledgling business, which packed and sold vitamins, at risk. But they turned it around, led by their charismatic and industrious patriarch, only to emerge as a leading manufacturing force in Australia. And because the family’s success came via leveraging global trust in Australian products, they offer a quiet and powerful rebuke of the anti-immigrant and identity discussion swirling around the surge in support for One Nation.

Advertisement

Theirs is a success born of being both Lebanese and Australian. But the success was not without its challenges. “We nearly lost everything overnight,” Aniss says. “We were completely screwed. And then Dad announced he had a solution. And we were waiting for something profound to solve our problem, but he goes: ‘Why don’t we make the medicine? Why are we packing it? I’ve decided we’re going to make it.’ Father and son Dr Elie Chami and Dr Aniss Chami, of Vitex Pharmaceuticals, at their new laboratory in Eastern Creek. Wolter Peeters “And we said, ‘Have you lost your mind?’” he says, laughing as he recalls the moment. Elie Chami has a wide grin on his face as he hears his son recount the moment, his eyes sparkling with the kind of excitement that grips a man of faith who has been proven right.

Advertisement

Not only did he succeed in dragging his family through the tortuous process of converting his makeshift factory into a pharmaceutical manufacturer, but he also emerged as a juggernaut in the industry. The family business supplies some of the biggest supplements brands globally, employs 400 people and is looking to have 1200 or more in future. So, how did a kid from rural Lebanon, who worked in factories and as a taxi driver upon his migration to Australia, build one of our largest manufacturers? Elie grins again when asked. “I wanted to be the best.” A western Sydney story Elie’s journey to Australia was not straightforward. As civil war brewed in Lebanon in the early 1970s, Elie’s parents left for Australia ahead of their children in hope of building a foundation for their family.

Advertisement

They left Elie and his siblings with their grandparents in the mountainous village of Syr in Lebanon’s north for nearly three years, forging in young Elie a drive to prove himself. “Other people have a father for their birthday,” he recalls. “Have their mother next to them going to school, taking them to church. Why not me?” The Chamis hosted Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Premier Chris Minns at the Vitex plant last month. Audrey Richardson At age 14, Elie followed his parents to Sydney in 1974 and was immediately put to work. First at a factory that made bathtubs, then another factory that made glass bottles in Waterloo. He worked alongside his father and studied English at night. And while he picked up skills that would later become important, these jobs were “never enough”. He moved on quickly to driving instruction and then became a taxi driver, nothing ever feeling right.

Advertisement

The lightbulb moment came during a trip to Lebanon. Intent on baptising his son at the church of his saint, Elie found his family and friends repeating a question: “Did you bring any Panadol?” It was common, particularly in the ’80s and ’90s, for Lebanese-Australians to visit Lebanon with baggage lined with Australian medicine, inaccessible to the small war-torn slice of the Middle East. Elie Chami at home. Sitthixay Ditthavong But very few saw a business opportunity in the question. “These people are hungry for medicine,” Elie remembers thinking. “They knew of vitamin C, vitamin D, multivitamin and fish oil, but had nothing. They heard of it, but they didn’t have the money to buy it.” Despite being an outsider to the industry, he was quickly connected with Jim Selim, the man behind Pan Pharmaceuticals. Himself a migrant from Egypt, the ambitious businessman saw in Elie a willing energy.

Advertisement

He handed him a briefcase of pills, a booklet explaining what they did, and instructed him to find buyers in the Middle East. So Elie bought a suit, “polished up” and was on the road with his trusty, arresting grin. It didn’t take long to secure his first contract, a buyer in Lebanon who leapt at the opportunity. Elie was off. He soon secured buyers across the region, and by the early ’90s, he had established himself as a capable salesman. Yet two decisions defined the trajectory of the business, which became known as Vitex – the first, for Vitex to do its own packing; the second, to manufacture its own pills. Selling Australia Both transitions were born out of Pan and Selim. But it was Pan’s collapse in 2003 that set Elie on his current trajectory.

Advertisement

The collapse came after the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) recalled 1600 of Pan’s products due to complaints of defective pills, leaving Elie and his fledgling company broken. At that point, Elie sat the family down in the dining room of their Hoxton Park home and declared that he wanted to make his own pills. They had, just a couple of years earlier, scraped together the money and equipment to begin packing, and had received their licence from the TGA after a thorough audit which included remodelling their facility. “Apparently you can’t have a bathroom open out to your packing room,” Elie says with a laugh. “How was I supposed to know?” The jump to making their own pills was an enormous move, both expensive and risky. The family put everything on the line to make the transition, but it was when Elie successfully turned a lolly machine into a tablet coater that Aniss thought they could make it work.

Advertisement

“That was the moment, for me, when I started to believe in him,” Aniss says. “You believe in God, you believe in yourself, but I believed in him from that moment. I said, ‘He must be Midas’.” Related Article NSW Votes ‘Not neanderthals or rednecks’: Inside the rise of One Nation in Sydney Between 2005 and 2016, Vitex expanded from one factory unit to eight, before moving from one mammoth facility to the next. “This is a family that keeps reinvesting and growing the industry for the Australian economy,” Aniss says. “It’s no longer about us getting rich; it’s us building a legacy for Australia.” Two prime minsters (Anthony Albanese and Malcolm Turnbull) and one premier (Chris Minns) have visited their factories, and the family says each one was stunned by their achievements.

Advertisement

Theirs is a story littered with themes often associated with migrant success, such as their perseverance, their willingness to suffer and their foresight. But, in recognising the commercial potential in Australian-made medicine globally, Elie and his family came to this fascinating intersection of opportunity and identity. As migrants, they understood the power of Australia, arguably more so than those already living here. “He knew how to sell Australia,” Aniss says. “He used to say to me, we aren’t selling medicine. We’re selling Australian provenance.” Elie adds, in Arabic: “We’re selling the name.” Asked how he feels about Australia, Elie stares at the vast expanse of suburban and industrial spaces outside his office window.

Advertisement

“What country can understand my ambition?” he says. “Lebanon definitely couldn’t. I always used to dream and believe nothing is impossible. “I want to prove that I came to this Earth not just to walk and go. I want to leave something here,” he says, stubbing his finger into the desk for emphasis. “I want people to think of me after a hundred years.”

title: Love watching Neil the seal? This doco unearths the truth about ‘nuisance’ animals
text:
Advertisement

CultureMoviesMIFF Love watching Neil the seal? This doco unearths the truth about ‘nuisance’ animals Nell Geraets August 15, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This year’s Melbourne International Film Festival has kicked off. Here we take a closer look at some of what’s on offer. See all stories .

If this year has made anything clear, it’s that we love “nuisance” animals. When Neil, the elephant seal, visited Seven Mile Beach near Hobart, thousands of people flocked to see him, including interstate travellers. When Jimothy, an abnormally round raccoon, was spotted zipping around the suburban streets of Seattle, he became an unofficial mascot for the local baseball team. And when the filmmakers of A24’s documentary Nuisance Bear arrived in Manitoba, they found themselves filming alongside legions of tourists, all desperately hoping to capture footage of the region’s migrating polar bears. Nuisance Bear documents the complicated coexistence between humans and migrating polar bears. But as adorable, funny or downright strange as it may be to see these wild animals encroaching on “human” spaces, Canadian filmmakers Jack Weisman and Gabriela Osio Vanden discovered there’s something more insidious going on beneath the surface. “The more famous an animal gets, the more likely it’s going to die because there are just too many people harassing it,” says Weisman, co-directer of Nuisance Bear. “It will become too comfortable with humans, and then it will cross that line. It’s always the animal that loses.”

Advertisement

He encountered this harsh reality when filming Nuisance Bear, a 10-year project that won the Grand Jury Prize for US Documentary at Sundance, and is now screening at the Melbourne International Film Festival. Shot in Churchill, Manitoba – the “polar bear capital of the world” – and the nearby Inuit community of Arviat, the film explores the uneasy coexistence between humans and migrating polar bears, as climate change delays the seasonal freezing of Hudson Bay. Loading Just like Neil and Jimothy, the Manitoba polar bears attract major attention as they meander through populated towns. However, the documentary demonstrates how general wildlife appreciation can transform into spectacle, putting both ourselves and the animals at risk. It goes beyond our actions – even our perception of wildlife is flawed. When picturing polar bears, most envision the pristine arctic, areas untouched by humans. But Weisman says this is a colonial idea used to push Indigenous people off the land. “Before colonisation, there were nomadic people moving all around. There were always people interacting with animals everywhere, and so it’s a newer idea that there’s this separation between ourselves and the wilderness.”

Advertisement

Related Article MIFF Striking hakas and alien appendages: Inside the new wave of New Zealand horror It’s largely because of this constructed distinction that we’re so fascinated with “nuisance” animals. They appear mysterious and “other”, Osio Vanden says, and therefore something people want to immortalise on camera. This, however, can transform into harassment or habituate animals to human spaces. “On one hand, I love seeing [Jimothy] emerge from the woods and show that not all raccoons look the same,” Osio Vanden says. “Witnessing animals’ survival abilities is very inspiring. But all these things are a double-edged sword.” Take Neil the seal, who, according to the Department of Natural Resources and Environment, racked up a damage bill of $45,674 thanks to his bollard-smashing and traffic-cone crunching antics. Meanwhile, some US wildlife officials have expressed concern over Jimothy fans desperately seeking selfies with the raccoon (who is believed to have a disorder called short spine syndrome) since this could disrupt his natural behaviours.

Advertisement

Neil, the seal, has become an Aussie icon. But could his fame do more harm than good? Rebecca Morris, Department of Natural Resources and Environment Tasmania Jimothy the raccoon went viral online because of his abnormally round body and long legs, which some believe to be the result of a disorder called short spine syndrome. Kiana Hall/Instagram The irony, Weisman says, is that these “pest” animals are actually more like us than we realise. The ingenuity required to survive alongside humans and thwart our efforts to drive them away rivals only our own. We may not look like a 1000-kilogram seal, and we may not love rubbish as much as Jimothy, but Weisman believes they still trigger deep reflection about how we live on the land and take up space. So, who is the real nuisance? It’s certainly not the animals, Osio Vanden says. “The bear in our film is constantly being pestered by crackers and cars when it’s just trying to go along its migration path. I imagine for most animals trying to navigate a human world, it’s super complex … We’re always thinking about how these things affect us, but how do we affect them? We’re a huge problem for ourselves and for all the living things we share this planet with.”

Advertisement

Related Article MIFF Young people are struggling like never before. These films ask why Nuisance Bear doesn’t point a finger at anyone in particular. While the Indigenous and non-Indigenous communities differ in their approach – the former generally support sustainable polar bear hunting while the latter tend to capture and relocate – the documentary doesn’t “pick a side”, other than, perhaps, the bear’s. Ultimately, Weisman hopes audiences never look at “nuisance” animals the same way. “When engaging with wildlife, they’re not just a spectacle. They look back at us. They’re affected by our behaviour. They’re sensitive – much more sensitive than humans are. We like to think that animals are not as intelligent as us because it justifies our cruelty. I just hope that people will look at ‘nuisance’ animals in a more nuanced and deep way.” Nuisance Bear will screen as part of MIFF on August 15 and 17.
